scope: Full-length review of the v72 weaker neutral halo and wider hand-containment candidate
summary: v72 passes all eight automatic non-human-review gates and is visibly lighter and temporally smoother than v71, but is not promoted because the 5px residual-arm feather produces a tiny active-coverage regression on exit frame 249.
evidence: The 660-frame output and comparison fully decode; protected content and pixels outside the safety region remain exact before encode.
Maximum neutral-halo strength falls from 0.21 to 0.16 while cleanup radius grows from 90px to 102px; plate-distance reduction is 0.181303 versus 0.205341 for v71.
Output ROI mean jerk is 1.626816, lower than v71's 1.680490, and full-frame mean jerk is 0.721601 versus 0.722189.
Every-frame reviews of 110--136, 235--255, 384--405, and 475--492 and dense three-frame reviews of 120--250 and 389--490 show no recognizable human hand leak.

A strict per-frame residual-arm area comparison finds 659 non-regressing frames and one frame-249 regression of 0.0000375601 image fraction; cumulative active area increases from 4.512778 to 4.921660.
The first contact-sheet command failed because the installed FFmpeg lacks drawtext; unlabeled fixed-order sheets (v71 left, v72 right) were generated successfully without modifying the video.
lessons: Neutral halo opacity and semantic hand coverage should remain independently tunable.
Even visually invisible coverage regressions at fade boundaries should block promotion when full containment is an explicit acceptance requirement.
Keep the accepted 4px residual-arm feather unchanged and widen only the weak neutral cleanup support.
limitations: Human review remains pending and the candidate is not published as the current showcase.
QuickTime continuous-playback control timed out after opening the file picker, so temporal review relies on full decode, jerk metrics, and dense contact sheets.
next_actions: Run v73 with the same 102px/0.16 neutral halo but restore the accepted 4px residual-arm feather, then require zero per-frame coverage regressions.
